title: On-site interactions in quantum thermal machines: efficiency, rectification and entanglement beyond local and global master equations
authors: Salvatore Araceli, Teddy H. M. Ong, Baptiste Debecker, Kai Müller, Oliver Lunt, Andrew J. Daley, François Damanet
abstract: Advances in experimental techniques have opened new routes for harnessing non-equilibrium dynamics in mesoscopic quantum systems. In this context, we study the impact of on-site interactions on the transport properties of a continuous quantum thermal machine composed of two coupled oscillators connected to two thermal reservoirs. In the weak system-reservoir coupling regime, where a long-standing debate concerns which reduced description should be preferred, we first show that the Redfield master equation (RME) provides an accurate and unifying framework that interpolates between two well-known limits: the \textit{local} and \textit{global} master equations. By relying on the Hierarchy of Pure States (HOPS), a numerically exact stochastic method, we then explore the full parameter space and show that interactions can be leveraged to tune the efficiency of the thermal machine at high temperatures (while leaving it essentially unchanged at low temperatures), induce non-reciprocal transport under asymmetric reservoir couplings, and generate steady-state entanglement within the junction. We derive expressions for system-bath correlators, such as heat and particle currents, consistently across different frameworks. Our work features on-site interactions to enhance the versatility of quantum thermodynamic junctions and clarifies the role of non-Markovianity and non-linearities in quantum transport.
summary: This paper analyzes quantum thermal machines by studying how on-site interactions modify key transport properties like efficiency and rectification. By comparing results from multiple master equation formalisms against an exact stochastic method (HOPS), the authors demonstrate that interactions enable novel functionalities, such as tunable efficiency and non-reciprocal heat flow.
main_problem: The study investigates how on-site interactions affect the efficiency, rectification, and entanglement properties of continuous quantum thermal machines.
main_result: Interactions can tune the machine's efficiency at high temperatures while leaving it robustly unchanged at low temperatures, and they are necessary to induce non-reciprocal transport and steady-state entanglement.
method: The authors compare results derived from multiple theoretical frameworks—including Redfield, Local, and Global Master Equations—against exact stochastic methods like HOPS.
model_or_system: The model is a continuous quantum thermal machine consisting of two coupled oscillators (sites) connected to two distinct thermal reservoirs (hot and cold). The system Hamiltonian includes an on-site interaction term ($U$).
key_observables: Efficiency ($\eta$), rectification ratio ($R$), steady-state entanglement (Log-negativity $\mathcal{E}_N$), heat currents, and particle currents.
important_parameters: On-site interaction strength ($U$), reservoir coupling strengths ($\kappa_\ell$), temperature ratios ($T_h/T_c$), and system frequencies ($\Omega_\ell$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the weak system-reservoir coupling regime for master equation derivations, though HOPS extends applicability. Comparisons are made between different approximations (LME vs GME).
figures_summary: Figures compare steady-state populations and fidelity across LME, GME, RME, and Exact methods; other figures show the dependence of power, heat currents, rectification ratio, and entanglement on temperature and interaction strength.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares various theoretical descriptions (LME, GME, RME) for open quantum systems dynamics. It then applies these tools to analyze thermodynamic quantities like efficiency and current flow, demonstrating the role of interactions in enhancing non-equilibrium features like rectification and entanglement.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles the fundamental problem of modeling open quantum systems where multiple theoretical approximations (LME, GME, RME) exist. The use of HOPS provides a powerful, numerically exact tool to validate predictions in complex non-equilibrium regimes.
